context: A 60-node force-directed network demonstrating how sqrt/linear/log scale choice distorts perception of node influence. Nodes are sized by influence (right-skewed, a few hubs) and colored by a continuous diverging sentiment scale (blue=negative, red=positive). A dropdown toggles the size scale and reheats the simulation.
first_impression: The network is moderately dense in the center but readable at a glance — hub nodes are clearly dominant and the diverging palette distinguishes sentiment without overloading categorical memory.
what_works: Hub nodes are unmistakably prominent under the sqrt scale, making the pedagogical point obvious without interaction; the neighborhood-highlight on hover is a strong cognitive aid that collapses a tangled center into a focused egocentric view. The continuous diverging palette avoids categorical color overload entirely.
what_doesnt: Community structure (Tech/Media/Policy/Science) is invisible — color encodes sentiment rather than community, so the four-cluster topology can't be seen at a glance, and the center reads as a uniform tangle rather than overlapping groups. Scale-change reheats the full simulation, causing all 60 nodes to rearrange simultaneously, which makes it hard to track individual nodes across scale transitions — the pedagogical payoff of 'see how size changes' is undermined by positional churn.
